Rejected: a desired reset with a time in the desired state of the deployment, which would also reach a gateway that is offline, but needs a persisted field in the cloud and outlives the resend of the deployment, while a new version of the deployment resets the gateway anyway. A gateway with an older engine answers the request with `unknown method`.

## Versions per deployment (2026-11-03)

**Event descriptions per version (DEP-04).** An update used to replace all event descriptions of a deployment with those of the new version. As the message name `<deployment>_<element>` is the same in every version, an instance kept on an older version with `drain` got the events of the new version: their condition, device and value variable applied to the element of its own version, and an event removed in the new version never reached it. Now an update replaces only the descriptions of its own version, and a device or import event correlates only with instances on the version of the description that matched (`CorrelationRequest.DeploymentVersion`, a filter in `MessageSubscriptions`); a description of an older version starts nothing, only the current version has start events. An instance on a version without descriptions of its own, which an engine before this change left running, takes those of the current version, so that existing drained instances keep getting the events they got before. The device groups of a deployment are kept per version as well (migration 14 rebuilds `deployment_device_groups` with the version, filling in the current one), and a changed group derives the descriptions again for every version that has them, from its own model and selections. A gateway gets those of the current version with its deployment; older ones it keeps as it got them. Rejected: a message name per version, which would break the stable event ids DEP-04 asks for, and descriptions per instance, which the event worker would have to load and evaluate once per waiting instance.

**Removing unused versions.** With `stop` and `restart` no instance stays on the older version, and its descriptions go with the update; with `drain` they go once no instance runs on the version any more, in the housekeeping. A version itself goes once no instance and no run refers to it, so after the retention removed the last instance on it, not when that instance ends (decided by the user): history and debugging of ended instances need the model of their version (DBG-13), and a restarted instance keeps runs on its former version. The current version always stays. Rejected: removing a version when its last instance ends, the wording of DEP-04, which would leave ended instances without their model.

**`keep_versions`.** The versions of smart service designs are releases, which `/deprecated/smart-services` lists all of and users delete themselves, as with smart-service-repository (SMS-03). A namespace with `keep_versions` keeps every version until the deployment is deleted; their event descriptions go all the same. The shipped smart-services sets it, and migration 15 marks a stored smart-services namespace once, as migration 12 did for `cloud_only` (decided by the user). Rejected: removing versions there as well, which would take older releases out of the list of the smart service designer.

## Managed deployments as dependents (2026-11-03)

**SEC-13.** A smart service instance manages the process deployments its modules created (`managed_by`). Such a deployment belongs to someone other than the instance's owner when it runs on a gateway, whose resources belong to the owner of the network (FOG-11), or after an owner change (SEC-11). Deleting the instance's owner removed the instance and left the deployment with a `managed_by` that pointed nowhere, and the dry run did not name it. Now the dependents of a user include the deployments of others managed by an instance deleted with the user, the user's own instances and those on the user's deployments, and the instances of others on such deployments. Whether they block or go is decided by their namespace (`user_deletion`), as for instances; the default rejects. With cascade they are deleted with their instances, on a gateway through the desired state, and their owners are notified with the cause. Deployments of the user that an instance manages go as the user's, not as dependents. One level is enough: only smart service instances have modules, and the processes they deploy have none.

## Runs as a ring buffer (2026-11-03)

**LONG-03.** Activities were a ring buffer per instance already (`max_activities`), but runs, incidents and element statistics went by age only, so an instance restarted often kept every run within a long retention. An incident ends its run, and element statistics are per run, so a limit on runs bounds all three: `max_runs` (default 100, `MAX_RUNS`, overridable per namespace like the other limits) keeps the newest runs of an instance with their incidents and element statistics, and the retention pass removes older ones per deployment, where it already trims by age; in the cloud this covers the incidents replicated from gateways too. The debug state sets `runs_truncated` when the oldest kept run is not the first. Rejected: trimming at every run start, as for activities, because runs grow by one per restart and the restart policy (INC-04) bounds them already; a pass per minute and batch is enough. The historical debug state does not carry the flag: its runs come from snapshots and the activity log, not from the stored runs.

## Storage report by part (2026-11-03)

**LONG-14.** The storage report counted rows of a fixed list of tables, without IO values, runs, element statistics and subtasks, gave a size only for the whole database, and kept the instances with the most history entries to the Prometheus metric, so a gateway never reported them. The tables of instances are now assigned to four parts, runtime state, history, outboxes and IO values (`store.StorageCategories`); rows are counted for all of them, and their size with indexes per part, on Postgres with `pg_total_relation_size`, on SQLite with the `dbstat` table, which the modernc driver provides. Models, deployments and their versions are not part of the report: they are definitions, not data an instance accumulates. A gateway sends sizes and the ten instances with the most activity entries with its status, and the cloud shows them under `storage` of `GET /networks/{id}`; the metric `storage_bytes{category}` carries the same sizes. `dbstat` reads every page of the database, so sizes are measured at most every five minutes, as often as a gateway sends its status. Rejected: `PRAGMA page_count` per table, which SQLite does not offer, and estimating from row counts, which misses the values that make a table large.

## Crash brake (2026-11-04)

**EXPR-03.** goja recurses natively over values a script builds; a built-in assigned as `toString` or an array nested a million times ends the process with `fatal error: stack overflow`, which no `recover` catches, and the trigger of the script (a due timer, a job whose lock ran out, an automatic restart after an incident, an uncommitted Kafka message, a gateway applying a deployment again after the cloud resent it) runs it again after the restart. The engine stays on goja; `pkg/crashbrake`, ported from moses, makes the crash a single one per process. With `SCRIPT_CRASH_DIR`, every script evaluation records its unit and goroutine in a memory-mapped register, released by `defer` so that a panic out of goja frees the slot, and `debug.SetCrashOutput` writes the crash report beside it. The next start, before anything runs, stops exactly the unit whose goroutine the report names:
- a script of an instance (runner, pre- and postscripts of module tasks): an incident at its element; an instance that is not running but has an automatic restart due crashed in that restart, which is cancelled;
- the condition of an event: the description is suspended (migration 17, column `suspended`, a new revision brings it to every event worker, and describing the same version again keeps it); the instances waiting for it get an incident, and so does an instance that reaches it later;
- the expression of a start timer, or a script of an instance whose creation the crash rolled back (a message or timer start, a schedule, a gateway instance): the deployment version is quarantined (table `quarantined_deployments`) and the deployment disabled. The quarantine also applies to a deployment created only after the crash: `ActivateVersion` disables it and computes no start timers while the version is not newer than the quarantined one. A module script of a deleted instance stops nothing, its unit has no version.

The deployment is marked faulty (`faulty_since`), which pauses automatic restarts and reaches the cloud from a gateway (SYNC-02), and its owner is notified once. The explicit reset lifts all of it and activates the version again; an update resets the restarts and resumes suspended conditions, but a quarantine is lifted only by a newer version, because the gateway resets the restarts also when it applies again the version that ended the process; enabling a quarantined deployment lifts the quarantine. Enabling or disabling a deployment that is not quarantined leaves its start timers as before. A decision that cannot be applied, e.g. without database at the start, stays in the directory for the next start. With several replicas each has its own directory, so each may crash once on the same script before its next start stops it. The register is locked with `flock`: a second process on the directory, such as `migrate` with the operating configuration, would reset the register and blame a crash on a unit of its own whose goroutine has the same id; it runs without the brake, `migrate` does not open it, and a failed start of the server frees it. The goroutine stack is capped at 256 MB once the brake is on, so that an overflow writes its report before the memory limit of the pod (1 GiB for the event role) kills the process without one. The runtime writes `fatal error: stack overflow` to stderr only; the crash output starts with the stack, where `runtime.newstack` marks the overflow. Two rounds of adversarial review with crashes in child processes found the rolled back instances and deployments, the gateway re-applying a quarantined version, the crashing automatic restart, the slots lost to panics, the shared directory and the lifted suspension; each has a test with a real crash or a mutation now. Rejected:
- stopping every unit in flight at the crash, or counting deaths without report: both stop innocent units, e.g. during a broker outage;
- a marker in the database: a second write per evaluation, and on SQLite no second transaction while the runner's is open;
- comparing the script source to decide whether an update fixed it: units would need the source or its hash at every evaluation site; a newer version, enabling or a reset is the user's signal instead;
- QuickJS (branch `feat/quickjs-script-runtime`), which contains these scripts without a crash: kept on goja for now, see "Script runtime" on that branch.

## Script blocklist (2026-11-04)

**EXPR-03.** The crash brake stops a unit, not a script: a smart service that deploys the same process with a crashing script hundreds of times, and starts it hundreds of times with random delays before the script, crashes each replica once per deployment. A blocklist of scripts closes that:
- **Entries:** the fingerprint of a script, a SHA-256 over the syntax tree goja's parser produces, without positions and without the source text it keeps for functions and classes; a script that does not parse is hashed as text. Comments, whitespace, inserted semicolons and redundant parentheses do not count, names and literals as written do. Decided over the exact text, which one space evades, and over an AST with normalised identifiers, which risks matching harmless scripts of the same shape. A first version hashed the token sequence of an own lexer; the review showed that every place where the lexer reads the source differently from goja hides code: a `//` comment ending at U+2028, which the lexer did not know, gave `value > 20 //<U+2028>crash()` the fingerprint of `value > 20`, so one crash would have blocked the default condition `true` of every tenant. Its recursion over nested templates also overflowed the stack before the brake marked the unit. The tree walk is iterative, because the parser limits nesting but not a chain like `a+a+...+a`. With the source, the reason, the origin (crash) and a revision, in table `blocked_scripts`. The crash brake records the fingerprint of the running script in its unit; the start that applies the decision adds the entry.
- **Validation:** a deployment with a blocked script is refused, checked again after the deploy parameters replaced inputs; a model save only reports it, as every validation issue. Smart services deploy through the same controller path.
- **Run time:** every evaluation looks up the fingerprint before it runs (sandbox, module scripts); a blocked script becomes an incident instead of running, also in instances that waited long before reaching it. Replicas learn new entries by polling the revision.
- **New entry:** the stored deployment versions are scanned in the background; a deployment whose current version contains the script is quarantined, and the running instances of every matching version are stopped with an incident at once (decided over stopping them only when they reach the script); conditions with the script are suspended. Owners are notified once per deployment.
- **Originator:** a crash also stops the smart service instance that created the deployment (`managed_by`) with an incident and quarantines every deployment it manages, which catches variants of the script the fingerprint misses. Deployments of gateways are left out, as in the search.
- **Version of a crashed instance:** a crash of an instance also quarantines its deployment version, unless a newer one is active, and stops its other running instances. Without it, a script that a mapping assembles at runtime (`prescript` as script mapping, e.g. with `Math.random()`) has a new fingerprint in every instance, and a process started hundreds of times crashes each replica hundreds of times. Decided over stopping only the crashed instance, as the brake did before, for the same reason the blocklist stops running instances at once.
- **Second review** (same day): a start timer expression that crashes while a smart service deploys rolls the deployment back with its `managed_by`, so the unit of a deployment now carries the smart service itself; a smart service waiting for its automatic restart after an incident was not stopped, its restart is now cancelled and its deployment marked faulty. Two replicas adding the same entry collided on Postgres (count, then insert); the insert now ignores a conflict.
- **Depth limit** (found in the second review, older than the blocklist): goja's compiler recurses over the syntax tree without a limit, and its parser limits nesting but not a chain like `a+a+...+a`; three million terms in a 6 MB model end the process in the compile check of a save or deploy, outside of the brake, at will. `script.Compile` refuses a tree deeper than 5000 levels (`script.MaxDepth`) before compiling; the sandbox and module scripts compile through it. The depth comes from the same walk as the fingerprint and is cached with it. 5000 leaves room for generated scripts and keeps the quadratic compile time of a chain below a second.
- **Order of a decision:** the stop of the unit, the blocklist entry, then the version and the originator, each in its own transaction; the entry also when the unit is gone since, e.g. a deployment deleted while the engine restarted. A failed step keeps the decision for the next start; applying it again is harmless.
- **Open** (second review): a regular expression that backtracked catastrophically was not interrupted by the sandbox timeout (regexp2 in goja), so event debugging over HTTP, which has no concurrency limit, could hold all 1024 slots of the brake, and a crash then named no unit; since the patched goja (see "Patched goja"), a match ends after a second, and the known native recursions no longer crash at all. Module prescripts are not compiled on deploy, so a 10 MB prescript deploys, and the search after a new entry parses it on every replica at once, about 400 MB. A crash in one user's instance of a shared deployment quarantines the version of the owner and stops the instances of all users.
- **Limits:** the first crash per replica stays, and a script changed beyond formatting is a new one; only the stopped originator and the quarantine hold against that. Each root instance of a smart service, and each deployment someone creates by hand with a variant, costs one crash per replica; the root can be restarted by its owner. The brake records a unit without its element when the element id from the model makes it too long for a slot. Gateways get deployments only after the cloud validated them, but keep no blocklist of their own until fogsync carries one.
- **Text by default** (decided 2026-11-04 after the reviews): the blocklist only pays off against moving to another script engine if the fingerprint is cheap, so `SCRIPT_FINGERPRINT=text`, the default, compares the text without `//` comments, and `tree` keeps the syntax tree. `text` costs about 0.3 us for a short script and 3 to 7 us for 5 KB, mostly SHA-256; `tree` 12 us and 0.5 ms. SHA-256 stays, because a hash an attacker can collide would let a crash block a harmless script of another user; SHA-512/256 was slower here, where the CPU has SHA instructions. Without a lexer, the text mode takes `//` for a comment only at the start of a line or after a space or tab, and with no quote and no slash after it on the line, and ends it at every JavaScript line terminator: where a lexer would be needed to tell, the `//` stays, so that a misread can only make a copy look different, never hide code. Copies that differ in spacing or indentation are other scripts in this mode; the version quarantine and the stopped smart service catch those. Entries keep their source and are matched by its fingerprint in the current mode as well, so that a change of the setting keeps them. A new entry is logged at level error with process, task and owner, by the one replica that added it; a removal at level warning.
- **Implementation:** `script.Fingerprint` (by text, or goja's parser without source maps; cached by a 64-bit hash of the source, not the source itself), `script.Blocklist` (empty: no fingerprint is computed), `bpmn.Process.Scripts` (shared by validation and the search; module scripts joined as `script.JoinParts` runs them), migration 18, `Engine.WatchBlocklist` (5 s, in both roles), `GET /blocked-scripts` and `DELETE /blocked-scripts/{fingerprint}` for admins. Removing an entry leaves quarantined deployments and stopped instances as they are. The attack itself is a test with a real crash in a child process: 20 deployments of a smart service with 60 instances, some waiting an hour before the script, and three copies of another owner; after the one crash nothing runs the script again and a new copy is refused.
- **Source maps** (found in the review): goja's parser reads the file a `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment names, `file:///dev/zero` until the memory runs out, in the sandbox, in module scripts, in the compile check of every save and deploy, and for `eval`. An OOM kill writes no crash report, so the brake could not stop it. Every runtime and compile now goes without source maps (`script.NewRuntime`, `script.Compile`).
- **Cost of the blocklist:** with an empty list one nil check. With entries, a cached fingerprint costs 15 ns for a short script and 0.4 us for 5 KB; an uncached one, once per process for up to 10000 scripts, 0.3 us and 3 to 7 us in text mode, 12 us and 0.5 ms in tree mode. The search costs 0.1 ms per deployment on SQLite and 0.7 ms on Postgres and runs only after a new entry; the revision poll every 5 s 7 us and 0.2 ms.
- **Compiled programs are cached** (2026-11-04): goja parsed and compiled every script at every run, and the sandbox compiled its `JSON.parse` shim each time as well. `script.Compile` now keeps the program per script, compared by its source and not only by its 64-bit hash, since on a collision another user's script would run; a goja program is bound to no runtime and runs in several at once. A program takes 12 to 20 times the memory of its source, so the cache holds up to 2 MiB of source, about 25 to 40 MB, starts over when full, and leaves out scripts above 64 KiB. The shim is compiled once. In tree mode the walk that measures the depth of the parsed script computes the fingerprint too, and `Sandbox.Run` compiles before it checks the blocklist, so that a new script is parsed once; with the crash brake on, the brake asks for the fingerprint first, which costs one more parse on the first run. A run of `value > 20` went from 20 to 8 us, of a 5 KB script from 350 to 29 us; the first run of a 5 KB script costs 0.6 ms in text mode and 0.65 ms in tree mode, where it cost about 1 ms before.
- **Crash brake cost** (decided to keep it on): 4.3 us per evaluation, 12 us with 32 goroutines in parallel, nearly all of it `runtime.Stack` for the goroutine id under a global lock of the runtime; against 2 to 10 ms per process step and about 250 us per event message through Kafka that is below 1 % and 2 to 5 %. The runner determines the id once per transaction.

## Patched goja (2026-11-04)

Some recursions of goja over data a script builds can only be stopped inside goja, and a regular expression that backtracks catastrophically ignores the interrupt of the sandbox (see "Script blocklist", open points). goja is patched without a fork of its repository, and the import path stays:
- **Decided:** `replace github.com/dop251/goja => ./third_party/goja`, a committed copy of the required version with the patches in `third_party/goja-patches` applied by `third_party/goja.sh`, which CI checks. It needs no flags, so Dockerfile, CI, the IDE and the arm builds work unchanged, and every patch is reviewed as a diff. `goja.EnginePatches()`, which the engine refers to, keeps a build without the patches from compiling. `replace` acts only in the main module: a repository that imports packages of the engine gets goja unpatched. A goja update through the require line alone changes nothing; the script has to run.
- **native-depth** (patch 2): a counter on the runtime at every recursion of goja's own Go code over script values that a test showed fatal under a 64 MB stack: the conversion to a primitive (a native as own `toString` or `Symbol.toPrimitive`, `Error.prototype.toString` with `e.name = e`, a nested array turned into text by `String`, `join`, a template, `+` or `sort`), `toLocaleString`, `flat`, `JSON.stringify`, the reviver of `JSON.parse`, `yield*`, `Export`, and every step to a prototype (get, set and `in` by name, index and symbol, 47 call sites, through helpers such as `protoGetStr`). Past 10000 levels the run ends with goja's `StackOverflowError`, which a script cannot catch, as with the call limit. Proxies and bound functions get the bound when created instead, counted together, because their targets cannot change and every operation follows the chain; a prototype can change after the fact, so a chain of prototypes is counted where it is walked. 30 shapes run as child processes in `engine_depth_test.go`, every one fatal without the patch; the cost was within the noise of the benchmarks, also for a script of prototype lookups. `Export` panics past the bound; the sandbox recovers it as an error. The crash brake tests raise `script.MaxNativeDepth` in their child processes to keep a real crash. Rejected: measuring the stack pointer, which moves when Go grows a stack; bounding prototype chains on `setPrototypeOf`, which two chains joined later exceed.
- **regexp-timeout** (patch 3): goja dropped every regexp2 error and reported no match; a timeout now ends the run with a `RegExpTimeoutError`, another regexp2 error with a `RegExpMatchError`, both uncatchable. The timeout is global (`goja.SetRegExpMatchTimeout`), because compiled patterns end up in programs that several runtimes share, and regexp2 reads it per pattern; the engine sets one second before any script runs. regexp2 still does not see the interrupt, so a run ends at most a second after its timeout. This closes the slots of the crash brake that hanging matches through event debugging could hold.
- **Rejected, tried in a throwaway module:** `-overlay` on the downloaded files, which Go refuses (`Files beneath GOMODCACHE ... must not be replaced`); `go mod vendor` with `-overlay`, which works but needs the flag on every build, test and vet and builds unpatched without it; editing `vendor/`, which the next `go mod vendor` drops silently; patching the module cache at build time, which `go mod verify` reports (`dir has been modified`) and the repository does not show; patching machine code at runtime (gomonkey), which needs inlining off everywhere, depends on the architecture and cannot reach the unexported methods that recurse; `go generate` writing the copy, which cannot run while the replace target is missing.

## Performance in the cluster (2026-11-05)

Basis: the logs of all four pods of `v0.33.1` in the cluster `senergy`, about 45 minutes after the rollout (10:32 to 11:17 UTC). Load was low: about 30m CPU and 60 MiB per engine pod, about 10m and 50 MiB per event pod (`kubectl top`). Nothing is changed yet; both findings are proposals.

**pprof in the cluster is not reachable with a developer account.** `PPROF_PORT=6060` is set and the pods log `pprof listening` on `127.0.0.1:6060`, but the account has no `create` on `pods/portforward` or `pods/exec` in the namespace, and the API server proxy is refused as well. Whether `kubectl port-forward` reaches the loopback binding (see `v0.18.0` in the project note) therefore remains unchecked; it failed on RBAC, not on the binding. Someone with the right: `kubectl -n automation-engine port-forward pod/<pod> 6060`, then `curl -o cpu.pb.gz 'http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=60'`.

### 1. The event role restarts its Kafka consumer four times a minute

Both event pods log `event worker topics` 181 times in 45 minutes, the count alternating between 16 and 17 every 8 to 20 seconds, each followed by `close kafka-go consumer`. The changes coincide to the second with `POST` and `DELETE /namespaces/processes/deployments` of the users `canary` and `snowflake-canary` (90 deploys and 90 deletes each in the window): their deployments carry event descriptions on a topic nobody else reads, so the topic set changes whenever the last of them comes or goes.

`Worker.Run` (`pkg/events/worker.go`) replaces the consumer whenever the sorted topic list differs. Both pods share one consumer group over all device topics (`pkg/server/events.go`, `kafkaConsumer`), so every change makes both pods leave and rejoin: a rebalance of the whole group, during which no event of any user is evaluated, and uncommitted messages are delivered again (dropped as duplicates by their message id).

Measured in the log of the group coordinator (`kafka-strimzi-cluster-broker-0`, readable with a developer account), 10:30 to 11:40 UTC: the group `automation-engine-events` went from generation 13768 to 14079, 312 rebalances in 70 minutes. Duration from `Preparing to rebalance` to `Stabilized` at the one-second resolution of the log: p50 0 s, p90 3 s, sum 418 s, about a tenth of the window without evaluation. Six of them took 30 s, the rebalance timeout: when a pod replaces its consumer while the group is still completing the previous rebalance, the old member sends no `LeaveGroup`, the coordinator waits for it until `Member ... has failed, removing it from the group` (13 times in the window), and meanwhile further restarts join, up to 8 members. The 3 s are probably `group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms` at its Kafka default, which applies when both pods leave at the same time and the group is empty for a moment; the broker configuration itself was not readable (no access to the Strimzi resource).

Locally (see "Local profiling" below) the same churn costs almost nothing: two event roles, the listener topic plus a second topic whose deployment is created and deleted every 7.5 s, 40 consumer restarts in 150 s, the rebalances took about 40 ms, and a looping listener on one event per second correlated 149 times in 149 s with two gaps of 1.6 and 1.8 s (baseline: 60 in 59 s, no gap above 1.02 s). The local Kafka sets `KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS=0` and has one broker and one partition per topic, so the local setup does not show the cost; the broker log in the cluster does.

- **Implemented (2026-11-05, not yet released):** `WorkerConfig.TopicGrace` (default 10 minutes, no environment variable); `Worker.Run` reads the needed topics plus those needed within the grace, so a new topic replaces the consumer at once and a topic no longer needed only after the grace. It applies on gateways as well, where it only keeps an MQTT subscription longer. Test: `TestATopicStaysSubscribedForTheGraceAfterItsLastDeployment`. Locally, with the same churn as above, six cycles caused no replacement after the first appearance of the topic, and the listener correlated 74 times in 74 s without a gap above 1.02 s. Originally proposed as: add a new topic at once, but drop a topic that is no longer needed only at the next full reload (`FullReloadInterval`, 10 minutes). A message on a topic without descriptions finds nothing in the index and is only read, decoded and dropped. Deploy/delete churn on a known topic then causes no restart; a description on a new topic still takes effect within the sync interval. This also removes most of the 30 s stalls, which come from restarts that overlap a running rebalance.
- **Rejected:** keeping every topic ever seen, which grows without bound; a fixed delay before every restart, which also delays new topics.

### 2. N+1 queries in the lists of the `deprecated/` layer

No request took longer than 630 ms; the only 5xx was one `503` on `POST /namespaces/processes/prepared-deployments` (canary). The slowest routes all come from the test accounts `shared-resources-test*`:

| Route | n | p50 | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /deprecated/smart-services/releases` | 35 | 298 ms | 630 ms |
| `GET /deprecated/smart-services/releases/{id}/parameters` | 2 | 533 ms | 533 ms |
| `GET /deprecated/repository/v2/processes` | 18 | 261 ms | 331 ms |
| `GET /deprecated/smart-services/designs` | 11 | 163 ms | 240 ms |

The native lists under `/namespaces/...` take 11 to 14 ms at p50.

- `releases()` in `pkg/deprecated/smartservices.go`: without `latest` and `ids` it loads all deployments and calls `GetDeploymentVersion` for every version from `d.Version` down to 1, also for trimmed versions, which return `ErrNotFound` only after the full call; `limit` and `offset` are applied in memory afterwards.
- `process()` in `pkg/deprecated/repository.go` and `listDesigns`: one `GetModelVersion` per model.

Each of these calls opens its own transaction and checks the right again through `readDeployment` or `readModel`. For a user who is not the owner that is an HTTP call to permissions-v2 (`Service.Check` in `pkg/permissions/permissions.go`), made while the transaction holds one of the eight connections of the pool (`POSTGRES_MAX_CONNS=8`). The list before it is already restricted to readable ids by `Access`, so the check per element repeats it. Under more load this turns into waiting for the pool, not only latency.

- **Proposed:** a store method per kind that returns the versions of a list of ids in one query, called inside the transaction of the list without a second check; for releases, page before loading versions where the order allows it.
- **Measured locally** (see "Local profiling"): 40 smart-services deployments of alice with 8 versions each, shared with bob through permissions-v2. `GET /deprecated/smart-services/releases` takes 165 ms for alice and 606 ms for bob (median of five); `limit=10` changes nothing (150 and 635 ms), because the versions are loaded before paging; `latest=true` takes 29 and 99 ms; the native `GET /namespaces/smart-services/deployments` 3 to 6 ms. In an execution trace over five requests of bob (3.2 s wall time) the engine waited 1.86 s in `net/http.(*Client).Do` of the permissions-v2 client, reached through `Store.Tx` → `GetDeploymentVersion` → `readDeployment` → `checkResource`, so with the transaction and its connection held, and 0.67 s for Postgres. In the CPU profile `GetDeploymentVersion` accounts for 54 % of the samples; the process used about a third of a core, so the request is bound by waiting, not by CPU.
- **Implemented (2026-11-09, not yet released):** `Controller.DeploymentVersions` and `Controller.CurrentModelVersions` read the versions of a list of ids in one transaction. The rights are read once with `Access` before the transaction, as the native lists do, and applied in the query (`Tx.DeploymentVersionNumbers`, `Tx.CurrentModelVersions`, joined with `deployments` or `models`); nothing waits on permissions-v2 while a connection is held. The release list pages over the version numbers and reads the content of the page only (`Tx.GetDeploymentVersions`). `addResources` takes the parsed process from the loaded version (`Engine.ProcessOf`) instead of one query per version for the cache key, and reads the resource checks once per deployment. `?ids=` of the releases reads its deployments with one list instead of one read each. A model or version deleted between the list and the read of its content is left out instead of failing the request. Tests: `TestVersionsOfAListFollowTheAccess` (SQLite and Postgres, also with one id per query), `TestReleaseListsOfASharedUserHoldWhatIsShared`, `TestProcessListOfASharedUserCarriesTheContent`, and the list in `changes` of `TestResourceCheckMarksChangedAndDeletedResources`.
- **Measured locally after the change** with the same data plus 40 process models with 3 versions each shared with bob, median of five, before → after: releases 121 → 16 ms for alice, 603 → 11 ms for bob; `limit=10` 596 → 10 ms for bob; `latest=true` 67 → 12 ms for bob; `/deprecated/repository/v2/processes` 89 → 10 ms for bob; designs 24 → 3 ms for alice. All 14 answers are byte-identical before and after. CPU of the release handler in a 10 s profile at the same request rate: 1.86 s → 40 ms. What remains is the two `Access` calls to permissions-v2 (list, then versions).
- **Not changed, same pattern:** `GET /deprecated/engine/deployment` (one `GetDeploymentVersion` per deployment for the SVG), the sync list with `extended=true` in `processsync.go`, and `GetDeploymentSource` per element of `extended-releases`. None of them appeared among the slow routes of the cluster logs.

### 3. Event processing under load (2026-11-09, local)

Load: 200 deployments of a loop whose device event (`x > 0`) correlates on every message, 200 whose conditions (`x > 100`, `x < -100`) never hold, all on the temperature service of one simulated device, one instance each; one event pod, one partition; devicesim sends one temperature message per second.

- **Throughput:** the event pod handles about 270 to 300 transactions a second and falls behind already at one message a second with 200 correlations each (consumer lag grows by about one message every few seconds). In a 10 s execution trace the consumer goroutine waited 7.67 s on Postgres, inside `Engine.Correlate` → `correlateInstance` → `Store.Tx`: every waiting instance is correlated in a transaction of its own, one after the other. CPU: 1.7 ms per correlation, mostly syscalls of the database round trips; condition scripts about 90 us per evaluation (15 % of the handler).
- **Per correlation of the loop** (from `pg_stat_database` and `pg_stat_user_tables`): about 13 rows in `activities`, 4 updates of `element_stats`, 3 of `tokens`, 1 insert and 1 delete in `subscriptions` and `changes`, 17 fetched rows; each statement is a round trip.
- **Locks:** the sync profile of the traces of both roles shows no wait on `sync.Mutex`, `RWMutex` or a semaphore; all blocking there is idle loops on tickers. The `mutex` and `block` profiles of pprof are empty, because the engine sets neither `SetMutexProfileFraction` nor `SetBlockProfileRate`.
- **Implemented (2026-11-09, not yet released):** migration 0021, index `subscriptions_token`. `DeleteSubscriptionsOfToken` runs on every flow a token takes, in both roles, and read the whole table `subscriptions`, the waiting messages and timers of all instances (404 sequential scans a second in the load above). With 20000 subscriptions one removal took 1.38 ms without the index and 0.08 ms with it; with the 400 of the load above the gain was 5 % more transactions. An older engine skips the unknown migration, so a rolling update is safe.
- **Implemented (2026-11-09, not yet released), parallel correlation:** `EVENT_CORRELATION_WORKERS` (default 4). `Worker.Handle` groups the qos 1 descriptions of a message by deployment and handles the groups on at most that many goroutines, the descriptions of a group one after the other as before, because a correlation can move an instance on to another event of its deployment that waits for the same message. Message names are `deploymentId_elementId`, so two groups never correlate the same instance. The message is committed when all groups are done, errors are joined. Gateways stay at 1 (one SQLite connection). Every description now evaluates its own deep copy of the message: the value reaches the condition script as a live object, and with the output of an analytics operator, which is handed over as it is, a script that wrote to it crashed the process with `concurrent map read and map write` once deployments ran in parallel (found by a verifier run; before, only qos 0 could reach it, and descriptions evaluated one after the other saw the changes of the previous one). Tests: `parallel_test.go` in `pkg/events`.
- **Tried and taken back (2026-11-09), activities of a transaction in one statement:** `Tx.InsertActivity` buffered the entries and wrote them with multi-row INSERTs before the commit, before every read and before any statement naming `activities` or `instances`. It took the activity INSERTs from about 13 to 2 per correlation (about 48 to 37 statements, counted with `log_statement=all` for one message), but with one worker the throughput stayed at 133 and 135 correlations a second against 140 of `HEAD`: each correlation is bound by its commit, not by its round trips. It needed rules a verifier run found gaps in (a failed write lost its cause on Postgres; on SQLite, which rolls back by itself when the disk is full, later statements ran outside the transaction), so the gain did not carry the complexity. Whether the round trips count in the cluster, with Postgres behind a network, was not measured.
- **Implemented, lock profiles:** `PPROF_MUTEX_FRACTION` and `PPROF_BLOCK_RATE` (default 0, off; rejected without `PPROF_PORT`).
- **Measured after the change** (same load, fresh data, 40 messages at once = 8040 correlations, event pool `POSTGRES_MAX_CONNS=8`, nothing else running; the earlier figures of this section were taken with other load on the machine): `HEAD` 140, 141, 140 correlations a second; with the change 239, 267, 263; with the change and `EVENT_CORRELATION_WORKERS=1` (batching only, see above) 133 and 135. The gain comes from the parallel commits alone; each correlation is bound by its commit (`WALSync`, `WALWrite`). With 4 workers the sessions wait on `Lock object` of `pg_database`, the global lock of the NOTIFY queue that every commit with `pg_notify` (the change stream of the live debugger) holds through its commit; an image without `pg_notify` was not faster (263 to 289), so the commit itself is the limit. Mutex profile over a burst: 276 ms of contention, nearly all runtime-internal, 1.7 ms on `sync.Mutex`; block profile: only waiting for worker slots, transaction ends and idle loops. The lock profiles cost about 5 to 10 % throughput.
- How many partitions the device topics have in the cluster, and so how many messages run in parallel there already, is not known here.
- Kafka showed 120 % CPU during the measurement; that was the JVM of `kafka-consumer-groups.sh`, started in the container for every lag query, not the engine.

### 4. Further profiling (2026-11-09, local)

- **Idle:** about 1 % CPU per role and 23 transactions a second with one simulated message a second; the statements come from the correlations of that message (each `Correlate` reads subscriptions and message start events) and from the retention, which walks all deployments once a minute (11 statements each). Nothing to change.
- **Engine role, device commands:** 300 instances of the thermostat example at once (two pessimistic device commands each). With the answers over Kafka, as devicesim sent them, 27 instances a second: the response consumer handles one answer after the other and was busy about 90 % of a 4 s trace (2.9 s waiting for Postgres). On the platform the connectors answer over HTTP (`METADATA_RESPONSE_TO`, port 8081), which the engine handles concurrently: 49 instances a second (about 100 commands) with `POSTGRES_MAX_CONNS=8`, 54 to 56 with 16; the block profile shows the goroutines waiting for a connection (195 s in total over the run). Mutex contention 6 ms on `sync.Mutex` in the run. No code change: the limit is the pool and the commits.
- **devicesim** answered one command a second: kafka-go's `Writer` waits up to its `BatchTimeout` (default 1 s) for a fuller batch on every synchronous write; now 10 ms. It also answers with a POST, up to 32 at a time, when `response_to` is an HTTP URL, which measures the path of the platform. The engine's own writer (service-commons) uses `BatchSize: 1` and is not affected.
- **Heap:** of 27 MB in use, 8.9 MB are the files of the Swagger UI, which `github.com/swaggo/files` writes into an in-memory webdav file system at start, in every process, gateways included. The engine imports it through `permissions-v2/pkg/client`, which imports the server package `permissions-v2/pkg/api` (for `httprouterembed.go` and `swaggergen.go`), and that imports `swaggo/http-swagger`; unchanged up to `v1.1.4`. A fix belongs into permissions-v2 (those two files into a package of their own).

### Smaller observations

- The request log writes the path without the query, so `latest`, `limit` or `add-usable-flag` of a slow request cannot be told from the log.
- `copyToDevelopers` can still hang without a timeout (developer-notifications client `v0.0.6`); it did not happen in the window.

### Local profiling

pprof works in Docker Compose through `docker compose exec`, since the image is Alpine with busybox `wget`. An override sets `PPROF_PORT` without touching the compose files of the repository:

```yaml
services:
  engine:
    environment: {PPROF_PORT: "6060", POSTGRES_MAX_CONNS: "8"}
  engine-events:
    environment: {PPROF_PORT: "6060", POSTGRES_MAX_CONNS: "4"}
```

```sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.platform.yml -f pprof.override.yml up --build -d --scale engine-events=2
docker compose exec -T engine wget -q -O- 'http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=20' > cpu.pb.gz
docker compose exec -T engine wget -q -O- 'http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/trace?seconds=5' > out.trace
go tool trace -pprof=sync out.trace > sync.pb   # also net, syscall: where requests wait
go tool pprof -top -cum sync.pb
```

A CPU profile alone misleads for the `deprecated/` lists: their time is spent waiting on permissions-v2 and Postgres, which only the profiles derived from the execution trace show.

## Analytics operators as event source (2026-11-09)

**SNRGY-5113.** The smart service "Thermostatsteuerung nach Lüftungsverhalten" handed its predictions to the process through the operator `event-operator-all`, an HTTP POST to the Camunda wrapper, which the engine does not have. A catch event without `messageRef` now takes a selection `{"pipeline_id", "operator_id"}` besides device, device group and import. At deploy the describer reads the pipeline with the token of the owner from analytics-pipeline (`ANALYTICS_PIPELINE_URL`, `GET /pipeline/{id}`) and takes the topic from `outputTopic` of the operator. The deployment is rejected when the pipeline is missing, not readable or not the owner's (`userId`), when the operator is missing, local or without topic, when the URL is not configured, or on a gateway. The cloud topic `analytics-<operator name>` is shared by every pipeline with an operator of that name, so the worker indexes the description by pipeline and operator and takes only messages whose `pipeline_id` and `operator_id` match, as kafka2mqtt-manager filters. The value is the object `analytics` of the message, without unmarshalling; the condition, `value_variable`, `variables`, QoS, the maximum age and the bound by the creation of the version apply as for devices, and the local variables are `event`, `age` and `msg_id`. A path is rejected: the condition reads the field it needs from the object. A smart service deployment with such an event stays in the cloud. The old format of `/deprecated/deployment` names the source as `selected_generic_event_source` with `filter_type` `operatorId` and `filter_ids` `<pipeline>:<operator>`, as event-deployment and the flow deploy dialog of the web-ui wrote it; the topic is ignored on input and empty on output. The old prepared deployment now also lists a message event without device criteria as `conditional_event` with empty criteria: process-deployment left it out, but the engine needs a selection for it, so such a model could not be deployed through the dialog at all. The deploy dialog of the web-ui (branch `feat/analytics-events`) loads the pipelines of the user, offers their cloud operators as the group "Analytics" for every conditional event, only when deploying to the platform, and sends the choice as that generic event source. The module `process_deployment` of smart services takes the same flat selection, and also `generic_event_source` of the iot option with `filter_type` `operatorId`, the form smart-service-module-worker-process read; a path there is rejected as everywhere else. The smart service designer of the web-ui offers, for every element of the deployed process, the operators of the flows of the analytics tasks before it, as `{"pipeline_id":"${<task>_pipeline_id}","operator_id":"<node id>"}`; the expression inside the JSON text becomes JavaScript like every other mapping. The debug view neither reconstructs these events nor reads their current value: the operator output is not read from Timescale.

The message format of the operators (`pipeline_id`, `operator_id`, `analytics`) is taken from its readers, kafka2mqtt-manager and the input mappings of the flow engine (`analytics.<output>`); the source of the operator libraries is not on this machine. Rejected: a callback endpoint, which needs a token in the pipeline configuration, the reason the old design had an admin token in the public content; the topic in the selection, which the owner could point at the output of a foreign pipeline; the field `time` of the message as the age, because devices count by the Kafka timestamp as well; local operators, whose output reaches Kafka only when the flow engine forwards it.

During a rolling update an event pod of an older version reads a new analytics description as a device description without device and service, evaluates operator messages against it and notifies the owner of a failed evaluation at most once an hour, until it is replaced.

## Error boundary events (2026-11-10)

**SNRGY-5130, BPMN-19.** The thermostat control writes set points per thermostat in a loop; a thermostat that does not confirm its value stopped the instance for every room with an incident. An error boundary event on a service task, script task or task now catches what the task raises while its token is in it, the job only after its last attempt. Extended beyond the ticket (device commands only) to every task that can raise an incident, on request. `runner.catchError` takes the incident errors of the task body, `failJob` the last failed attempt; both move the token to the boundary event (`continueAtBoundary`), which is entered like any element, sets its local variables, applies its mappings and leaves. The job is deleted with its sub-tasks, so that a late answer finds nothing. The history reuses `task_failed` with `caught_by` instead of a new kind, so that the debugger of the web-ui needs no change; its replay now also records the error of every `task_failed` at the element, as `RecordElementError` does live, since without incident nothing else shows it.

Variables: `error_message`, `device_id` and `service_id` are local to the boundary event; `camunda:errorMessageVariable` writes the message to an instance variable too. Rejected: `device_id` as instance variable, which would overwrite a loop variable of the same name. The device of a device command comes with the failure: `engine.WithVariables` around the error, `FailTaskError` for asynchronous answers, the sub-task looked up by its id on an error answer. A timeout carries no variables; the task type names them through `FailureVariables` from its only sub-task, or the only one without result, before the job is deleted.

Caught: mappings, scripts, `resultVariable`, job creation (task type forbidden in the namespace), the last attempt including permanent errors and timeouts, normalization of the task output, LONG-08 limits. Not caught (`incidentError.uncatchable` or outside `catchError`): outgoing flow conditions (the task is complete then), the token limit at entry, crash-brake incidents and blocked scripts (`script.ErrBlocked`; such a script must not run on, also not over the error path), a task type this engine lacks (during a rolling update an older replica would otherwise send the token down the error path) and errors of the boundary event itself. Variables of a failure are normalized like task output, and `error_message` is always the message, not a variable of the failure with that name. `Cycles` starts its search at tasks, not at boundary events, so that a loop back to the task is found also when the boundary event comes first in the document. Instance variables written before the error stay, as in Camunda with `BpmnError`. Reachability for inclusive joins and the cycle check follow the edge from the task to its boundary event (`Element.Successors`). `errorRef` and `camunda:errorCodeVariable` are rejected rather than ignored, so that telling errors apart by code later changes no deployed model.

## Watches of device groups (2026-11-11)

**SNRGY-5132, TASK-27.** Smart services watched the members of a device group through a generic `watch_request` on the public gateway (`GET .../device-repository/device-groups/{id}`, `hash_type: deviceids`), which runs under the HTTP policy of the namespace and names the host of the platform in the model. The watcher now takes `watcher.watch_device_group`: the id of a group, as text or JSON string, or its IoT option `{"device_group_selection":{"id":...}}` as the start form gives it. Criteria come first if both are present, the group before a generic request, as the worker took the first variable present. The task reads the group with the token of the owner through the device-repository client, uncached, so a group the owner cannot read fails the task, and stores the hash of the sorted `device_ids` as baseline; device-repository leaves out devices the owner may not execute, as for the read the generic watch made. The watch stores the group in `watches.device_group_id` and the members of its last check in `watch_devices` (migration 23); its request stays empty.

Checks are announced, not polled. The consumer of `device-groups`, which already recomputes event descriptions (DEP-08), first makes the watches of the group due (`next_at = now`); a new consumer of `devices` in the same consumer group does so for a `DELETE` with the watches whose last members contained the device, because device-repository keeps a deleted device in the stored group and announces no change of it, but no longer returns it. The loop of the watches checks them as any due watch, by claim, so one replica reads each. After a successful check the watch is parked until the recheck (`WATCHER_DEVICE_GROUP_RECHECK`, 24 h), which finds a change whose announcement was missed, e.g. while device-repository could not reach Kafka; the parking is a compare-and-set on the time its claim set, so an announcement during the check keeps it due. A deleted group records the error and is parked too, since its recreation would be announced; any other failure, a failed start of the procedure among them, is retried after `watch_interval`, as before. The task checks the watch once right after storing it, for a change announced between its read and its commit. Without Kafka (`KAFKA_URL`, `DEVICE_GROUP_TOPIC` or `DEVICE_TOPIC` empty) nothing announces, and the watch is checked by interval like the others.

Rejected: hashing the device ids of the Kafka message, which saves the read but ignores the filter by access and could not see a deleted device; polling the group by `watch_interval`, which the ticket offered first and which the announcements reduce to the daily recheck; making every watch of a group due on any device deletion, which costs one read per watched group for each deleted device. A device that leaves a group only through a change of rights is announced neither on `device-groups` nor on `devices`; the recheck sees it. Gateways do not run the watcher: `smart-services` is cloud only, `processes` does not allow the task type, and the process module of the gateway sets neither `DEVICE_SELECTION_URL`, without which the type is not registered, nor `KAFKA_URL`. While replicas of older engines run beside newer ones, an older one may claim an announced group watch and record an error for one interval, as it has no request to send.

## A cloud that goes back (2026-11-11)

**SNRGY-5066, SYNC-03.** A cloud that lost the state of a network, a new one after a move above all, answers the next status or batch of the gateway with a position behind the one the gateway has acknowledged. The gateway took the position but kept its batch in flight, which it releases only on an acknowledgement at or past that batch, so it sent the stream again only after its resend time (30 s by default, doubling up to 5 min while unacknowledged). It now also releases the batch when the cloud goes back behind the position acknowledged before, and sends from there at once; a repeated acknowledgement of the same position still waits. Found through the import tests, which under `-race` waited longer than their 10 s: besides the gateway, they cut off the first cloud while a batch could still be in flight, which is the 30 s resend by design, and the first one waited for a batch that happened to go out after the switch; they now wait for the acknowledgement before the switch and send the status explicitly. The data race of the long offline test was `Engine.SetClock` on a running engine; the clock is now an atomic pointer, as `restart_test.go` does the same.

## Audit against the requirements (2026-10-20)

Every requirement id of `docs/requirements.md` (242) was checked against code and tests, together with the gaps of the milestones above and the engine items of `OPEN-ITEMS.md`. None is missing entirely: 186 are implemented, 47 partly, 3 differ by a decision recorded above, 6 are tasks of other repos or of operations. Defects 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 were reproduced with tests in a copy of the repository, the others read from the code.

### Defects

All fixed on 2026-10-20, each with a test that failed before the fix; the decisions the fixes needed are in "Decisions of the fixes" below.

1. **The cloud runs the restarts of gateway instances (FOG-07).** `store.Tx.UpsertReplicatedInstance` copies the `restart_at` of the gateway into the cloud row, and `Tx.DueRestarts` has no `network_id` filter, so `Engine.restartInstance` executes the instance in the cloud as well. The comments in `pkg/fogsync/protocol.go` and `gateway.go` ("restarts are the gateway's own") describe the intent, not the behaviour.
2. **Removed modules leave their resources on the gateway (SMS-12, SMS-06).** `modules.Remover` deletes deployments and instances through `store.Tx.RemoveResource`, which removes only the cloud rows; the desired state of the gateway (`network_desired`) never learns of the deletion, unlike `Controller.desireDeletedDeployment` and `desireInstance(..., true)`.
3. **A gateway offline for more than an hour can lose the end of an instance (LONG-07, LONG-10).** The protection of not yet synchronised instances (`unsynced`, `pkg/store/sync.go`) rests on rows in `changes`, which `PurgeChanges` removes after `ChangeRetention` (1 h) whether the cloud acknowledged them or not. Retention or storage budget may then delete an ended instance whose end never reached the cloud, and the snapshot after the reconnect makes the cloud delete its copy, which it still holds as running. `TestTheCloudLearnsTheEndBeforeTheGatewayTrims` covers only short offline periods.
4. **A gateway one protocol version behind gets nothing from the cloud (SYNC-11).** The cloud accepts gateways in `[Version-window, Version]`, but stamps its own `Version` on every downward message (`cloud.go`), and the gateway drops every message whose version is not its own (`gateway.go`). After a protocol change, `SYNC_PROTOCOL_WINDOW` therefore does not let cloud and gateways be updated one after the other.
5. **An update that changes only the deploy parameters is ignored (DEP-04, DEP-01).** The "nothing changed" check of `Controller.PutDeployment` compares XML, SVG, name, description, model version, incident handling, retention and selections, not `Parameters`. It also hits updates through `deprecated/deployment`, which turn changed timers and inputs into parameters, and the updates of `process_deployment` modules.
6. **An update with `restart` fails as a whole if a running instance cannot be restarted (RUN-11, DEP-04).** `Engine.restartInstance` restarts at the start event without definition; an instance of a process that starts only through a message or a timer makes the whole update fail with 400. A restart after an incident fails the same way and only notifies the owner.
7. **The migration checks business keys per Camunda deployment, not per tenant (MIG-02).** `pkg/migrate/process.go` counts the uniqueness of a key per deployment; two running instances of one user in different deployments with the same key get the same id, the second is reported as existing, not restarted, and its IO values attach to the first.
8. **Deleting a user leaves their deployments and instances on gateways (SEC-08).** `Tx.DeleteOwned` deletes the cloud rows directly, without the desired deletions on the gateways.
9. **Cleaning up a network leaves its rights in permissions-v2 (SYNC-07).** `Tx.DeleteNetwork` removes rows with plain SQL, past `queueRemovals` and the change stream.
10. **The migration report drops rewritten and to-be-checked findings (MIG-04).** Only `Unsupported` is kept (`deprecated/deployment.go`, `migrate/process.go`), so rewrites such as `R/P1D` → `P1D` or five-field cron pass silently; only `POST /namespaces/{ns}/convert` returns the full report.

11. **The cloud ran the schedules of gateway deployments (FOG-05, RUN-07).** Found while fixing 1: `Engine.fireSchedules` started instances of a gateway deployment in the cloud, and nothing rejected such a schedule.

A documentation defect was corrected right away: `NOTIFIER_URL` on a gateway is `http://{gateway}/notifications-v2`, the notifier client appends `/notifications` itself (FOG-08); README and `OPEN-ITEMS.md` named the full path.

### Decisions of the fixes

- **Restarts of gateway instances** (1): the cloud keeps `restart_at` of a gateway instance only for display; `DueRestarts` and `NextRestartDue` consider cloud instances only.
- **Change stream on a gateway** (3): `TrimChanges` replaces `PurgeChanges` in the housekeeping. Up to the acknowledged position it removes by age as before; after it, only entries followed by a later one of the same instance. The cost: while offline, ended instances keep their runtime rows and the budget can trim only their history, so a gateway that ends more instances offline than its budget holds fills up instead of losing ends the cloud has not seen. Rejected: a fog-specific longer `ChangeRetention`, which only moves the limit.
- **Protocol window** (4): the cloud writes to each gateway in the version that gateway reported, if it lies in the window; a gateway accepts only its own version. All downward messages pass `encode` in `protocol.go`, where a future version converts to older formats. Consequence: a protocol change updates the cloud first, then the gateways one by one.
- **Network cleanup** (9): resources of a removed network are deleted one by one through `DeleteDeployment` and `DeleteInstance`, so rights, module removals and tombstones follow as for any deletion.
- **Deletions reaching gateways** (2, 8): module removal and the undo of a module go through `Controller.RemoveResource`, user deletion desires the deletions in the same transaction as `DeleteOwned`; both share `desireDeleted` with the deletion through the API. Instances of a user's own gateway deployments are not desired separately, the gateway deletes them with the deployment.
- **What counts as a change of a deployment** (5): name, description, model id and version, XML and SVG as resolved, incident handling, retention, selections, parameters, and a given source. Not: the update strategy, owner and network (refused), `managed_by`. Parameters and selections compare by effect, so empty and missing maps are equal. Such updates now need an `update_strategy`; the old deploy route sets `stop`, modules set their own.
- **Restarts** (6): a restart, after an update, an incident or through the API, begins at the start event that began the run, read from the element statistics of the run, if the version still has it; otherwise at the start event without definition. An instance that still cannot be restarted is stopped at an update with the reason in its run, and its owner is notified; the update goes ahead. After an incident it stays ended with its incident, as before. Rejected: failing the update, which let one instance block the new version. Open: the start element should be recorded on the run itself; replicated gateway instances have no element statistics and fall back to the start event without definition.
- **Schedules of gateway deployments** (11): rejected with 400 on create and on move; existing ones (e.g. from a migration) are skipped by `DueSchedules`. Rejected for now: sending schedules to the gateway, a new feature; process-scheduler had none for gateways either.
- **Instance ids of the migration** (7): a business key becomes an id only if exactly one running instance or fog start has it and no earlier step of the run took it; otherwise the id is generated from the Camunda or process-sync ids. A later run recognises an instance migrated under its key by namespace, owner, deployment, network, start time from the Camunda history and start values; candidates it cannot tell apart are left to decide, none is restarted. Fog starts now run right after the running instances, because module delete references resolve business keys through the ids assigned in the run; an ambiguous reference keeps its URL and is left to decide. Remaining limits: smart-service instances keep their old ids without a check against those the instance steps took, and without Camunda history the start time is not compared.
- **Migration report** (10): `DeploymentInput` returns the conversion with the input; every migrated deployment and release reports its findings as `rewritten`, `check` and `unsupported` items of kind `model`, which do not change the exit code.
- **`MIN_TIMER_DURATION` for cycles** (found after the audit): the deploy check covered literal durations only, so `R/PT1S`, cron `* * * * * ?` at a timer start, a schedule `* * * * * *` and timer expressions started or continued every second. Decided: the minimum also applies to cycles, as a limit at runtime where the due time is computed (`timer.NextNotBefore`, `timer.NextScheduled`, `Engine.earliestDue`), not as validation. A due time is never earlier than the minimum after the previous due time, or after now without one; an interval is stretched to the minimum, a cron takes its first time at or after that point. Counting from the previous due time rather than from the firing keeps `*/5 * * * * ?` at 5 s when the scheduler fires late. Computed durations of intermediate timers are limited the same way, consistent with the deploy rejecting the literal; dates are not limited. Rejected: validating cycles at deploy, which misses expressions and schedules; rejecting cron with seconds, which forbids `*/30 * * * * ?` as well, although Camunda models and process-scheduler accepted seconds, so migrated models and schedules using them would fail. Consequence: after a downtime the missed occurrence fires once and the next follows from the firing as before, so two starts can be closer than the minimum once.

### Partly implemented

Open tasks of the engine, not yet decided whether and when. The id says where the requirement is.

- **Validation:** the sandbox has no memory limit (EXPR-03, known since M1). Since 2026-11-03 the condition of a device or import event (`senergy:script`) is checked on save and deploy like every other script (BPMN-18, EXPR-01): it has to compile in goja, as the event-worker ran it with `RunString` and the event role runs it now; one that does not and contains `${` is reported as JUEL with a JavaScript example on its value variable. An empty condition stays allowed, it triggers on every value. Models deployed before keep running; a failing condition shows as an error of the evaluation, as before, and the next update of such a deployment is refused until the condition is fixed. The join semantics of the inclusive gateway are not compared with Camunda, in particular with loops (BPMN-15, known since M1).
- **Namespaces:** a changed namespace does not mark deployments that no longer fit (NS-03); there is no default update strategy per namespace (NS-07); the setting `device_selection` is stored but enforced nowhere (NS-11).
- **Models and deployments:** no rights filter `p` on model lists as in `/v2/processes` (MOD-01); no version distance (MOD-06, known since M1); since 2026-11-03 event descriptions are kept per version and unused versions are removed (DEP-04, "Versions per deployment"); `task_info` carries `deployment_id` next to the deprecated `process_definition_id` since `9747e43`, which goes once moses has an image with the field; `{{DefinitionId}}` is not rewritten but accepted as alias at runtime, untested (DATA-04).
- **Tasks and incidents:** module workers' flags `allow_msg_events_in_fog_processes` and `allow_imports_in_fog_processes` were not taken over; processes with device events now always go to the gateway (TASK-29); incident variables above 4 KiB are cut like the history (INC-06).
- **Events:** offline periods of a gateway are not marked in the reconstruction, and on a gateway `evaluate_events` evaluates nothing, because event debugging is wired only with Timescale (EVT-13).
- **Debugging:** the wait of a device command lacks the completion strategy, module tasks show no progress (DBG-02); wait reasons at historical steps are thinner than live ones, without event sources and subtasks (DBG-13); no interventions on gateway instances (DBG-17).
- **Rights and users:** the owner right is restored only with `PERMISSIONS_KAFKA_TOPIC`, which the deployment does not set (SEC-10, `OPEN-ITEMS.md`); signatures are verified only with `KEYCLOAK_CERT_URL`, for requests other than the live stream only with `VERIFY_TOKENS` as well, and the check against Keycloak itself has no test (SEC-04).
- **API:** paging is not uniform, activities use `after_seq` without total, several lists return plain arrays (API-06; the comment in `pkg/model/common.go` claims otherwise).
- **Synchronisation:** no "offline since" and no alert for gateways without contact (SYNC-12). A deployment the gateway marks faulty is reported upwards since 2026-11-03 (SYNC-02, "Faulty deployments of gateways").
- **Smart services:** stop and restart in an update apply only to running instances, so instances whose setup has finished are drained (SMS-03).
- **Operations:** no metric of the response time of device commands (OPS-05); spans carry no run id (OPS-07); acceptance on an arm64 gateway open (LONG-15, FOG-04). The release pipeline exists since `f4bddc7` (`prod.yml`, tags on `main`, CLI-06, FOG-02).
- **Migration:** watches of smart-service instances are not migrated, maintenance procedures of migrated instances stop with the old watcher (MIG-01); owners can be assigned only per old owner value, not per resource (MIG-09). Both matter only if the migrated data reaches the replacement cluster; the old data and the migration job are gone (`OPEN-ITEMS.md`, "Rollout").

### Behaviour that differs from the requirements without a recorded decision

Recorded here so that it is a decision; changing it would be a new task.

- Optimistic device commands send first and complete afterwards; a failed send is retried or becomes an incident instead of being only logged (TASK-01).
- Groups with `sequential` or `round_robin` take the task timeout as the answer window of one try and count retries per device (TASK-06, TASK-07; `docs/device-command-groups.md`).
- `MIN_TIMER_DURATION` (default 5 s) restores the minimum of process-deployment and extends it to cycles, schedules and computed values at runtime ("Decisions of the fixes").
- A timer that the old designer leaves empty gets the time of the old deploy dialog written into the model on deploy (`pkg/deprecated/timers.go`), instead of becoming a parameter.

### Superseded statements above

- M4 decisions and gaps: DBG-17 is implemented, and the search in the history covers variable values (both 2026-10-30, "Search in the history and interventions").
- M1 gaps: CI with the drift check exists (`.github/workflows/tests.yml`), the client covers the whole API (`client.Client` embeds `api.Controller`), EVT-08 has its metric, the MIG-05 comparison exists; open from that list are the memory limit, the BPMN-15 comparison and MOD-06.
- M2 gaps: the ongoing repair of the owner right came with M3 (only with `PERMISSIONS_KAFKA_TOPIC`); dependants via modules came on 2026-11-03 ("Managed deployments as dependents").
- M3 status: `GROUP_SCHEDULER` also knows `round_robin`, and the timeout is no longer the job timeout for groups (`docs/device-command-groups.md`).
- M4 decisions name `pkg/live.Hub`; it is `pkg/debug.Hub` (see "Cleanup").
- README: instances with modules are exempt from deletion by retention, not from trimming their history; on a full disk `/ready` reports the error, `/health` does not. Both corrected on 2026-10-20.
- M6 c: deployments with `network_id` and `prefer_fog_deployment` apply only to namespaces without `cloud_only`; `smart-services` never runs on a gateway ("Namespaces kept from gateways").
- M3 gaps: with `update_strategy=drain` instances of an older version keep the event descriptions of their version since 2026-11-03 ("Versions per deployment").
- Interventions (DBG-17): the sync protocol has a request that writes since 2026-11-03, `reset_restarts` ("Faulty deployments of gateways"); interventions on gateway instances are still refused.
- M1 gaps and "Partly implemented": the release pipeline exists since `f4bddc7`, and `task_info` carries `deployment_id` since `9747e43` (both corrected in place on 2026-11-03).
- M7 status: the Kong redirect and the migration ran on 2026-10-22; since 2026-11-02 the old stack and the migration job are removed from the deployment, a rollback to Camunda is no longer possible.
- M5 decisions and status: `smart-services` no longer sets `forbid_cycles` (decided by the user on 2026-10-22, during the migration). Three designs on the platform loop in their sequence flow and could not be migrated otherwise; every new run still removes the modules of the previous one. The setting stays for a namespace that wants to be stricter. A namespace stored by an earlier version keeps its value; the admin API changes it.

### Before this file is removed

This file is to be dissolved once the open items above are settled. Its decisions and rejected alternatives move to `docs/` or the README first; recorded only here are, among others: Postgres and SQLite from the start (millisecond `BIGINT`, JSON as `TEXT`, Mongo rejected), variable scopes after Camunda's `AbstractVariableScope`, globally unique instance ids, the NS-05 interpretation of permissions-v2 (`shareable`, `initial_rights`, `topic_default_permissions`), the event worker coupled through the database instead of Kafka or the API, the library choices with their licences (coder/websocket ISC, paho EDL-1.0, mongo-driver Apache-2.0, modernc SQLite without cgo), the rejected per-namespace module policy, the deviations of device commands from the workers, the rejected old sync protocol and sync role with leader election, the read-only gateway API, command correlation in the database, the dropped internal worker routes, the rejected migration through the old APIs, the rejected deployment per release, and the package consolidation. README and `OPEN-ITEMS.md` point to this file in their first lines.
